blocks.text: Overview

This exercise is for the Executive Vice President, Evidence role at Evidence Action. It is delivered in two stages. Stage 1 (this packet) is self-contained. The information in this document is representative of a real Evidence Action program, but parts of it have been fictionalized so the challenges presented are illustrative, not live questions.
Estimated time: 2 to 3 hours for Stage 1. The full exercise across both stages is designed for approximately 4 hours. We are not testing how quickly you work; please use the time you need.

Format: use any format you prefer. Write your response in the box at the end of this page, or attach it as a PDF or Word document. After you submit it you will be asked to select your recommended option, and you will then receive the Stage 2 materials. You will not be able to change your Stage 1 submission after that.
AI use: you may use AI tools. We require a disclosure at the end of your response describing what tools you used and how. See the questions below.
Scenario

You are the new Executive Vice President, Evidence at Evidence Action. You joined six weeks ago. You report to the CEO and sit on the Global Leadership Team, with the Monitoring, Learning and Evaluation, cost-effectiveness, and technical/epidemiology teams reporting to you.

Evidence Action has stage gates for approving new programs and for moving a program from pilot to scale. What we have not had is a consistent standard for the decision that comes next: whether to hold a launched program where it is, or expand it, and on what evidence.

Our Multiple Micronutrient Supplementation program in Nigeria has reached that decision. The pilot has closed, the country team has completed its analysis, and a recommendation is expected from you. It will not be the last decision of this kind, and the CEO has asked that your recommendation come with the beginnings of a standard we can apply to the next one.
The materials below are what the program team, the cost-effectiveness team and the country office have shared with you.
Background: the MMS program

The Nigerian government has integrated Multiple Micronutrient Supplementation (MMS) into its national guidelines and is exploring how to scale it. Evidence Action provides technical assistance to the Government of Nigeria on a scalable MMS delivery model.

MMS is a daily supplement containing 15 vitamins and minerals (the UNIMMAP formulation, which carries 30mg of iron per tablet), recommended by the WHO for pregnant women to reduce maternal anemia and improve birth outcomes. Compared to the current standard of care (daily Iron and Folic Acid, or IFA, supplementation), MMS has been shown in meta-analyses to reduce stillbirths by approximately 9 percent, small-for-gestational-age births by approximately 8 percent, and low birthweight by approximately 12 percent.

The benefits of MMS depend on actually taking the pills. The published evidence suggests increasing health benefits as pregnant women consume more pills. Internal modeling has shown that at 120 of the recommended 180 pills over the course of pregnancy, the full benefits are realized. Below this, the related benefits are lower and the intervention becomes less cost-effective.

There was essentially no existing evidence on whether pregnant women in this context would reliably consume MMS at these levels under the proposed delivery model. The evidence base on health outcomes assuming consumption does not include detail on whether pregnant women adhere in real-world LMIC contexts.
Findings from the pilot are intended to inform whether and how we scale MMS in Nigeria, and whether we expand MMS to other priority countries.
Context: antenatal care (ANC) in Nigeria
A few features of the ANC context shape what is feasible to deliver and to measure:

items: Most pregnant women do not attend ANC until their second trimester. First ANC visits most commonly occur in the 4th or 5th month of pregnancy, with some later.

Pregnant women vary widely in how often they return for follow-up ANC visits. Many attend two or three visits over the course of pregnancy; some attend only once; a smaller share attend more frequently.
Health workers at pilot facilities typically see 30 to 60 pregnant women per week, and the first ANC visit takes 1 to 2 hours and covers a broad set of topics.

Government ANC facilities in the pilot Local Government Areas (LGAs) are predominantly small rural primary health centers, with a smaller number of secondary facilities. Pregnant women travel from dispersed geographies to attend ANC visits.

blocks.text: The pilot

In order to generate evidence about the feasibility of delivering MMS and the adherence rate among users, a pilot study of MMS was developed. The pilot ran across approximately 90 government ANC facilities in 6 LGAs in Federal Capital Territory and Oyo State, enrolling approximately 2,900 pregnant women over a five-month window.

The delivery model replaced the standard 30-day IFA course distributed at each ANC visit with a one-time distribution of a 180-tablet bottle of MMS at the pregnant woman's first ANC visit, intended to last the remainder of her pregnancy. Health workers were trained on a distribution and counseling protocol, and recorded distribution and consumption in a new MMS-specific register. Women received counseling materials, SMS reminders and a paper consumption-tracking calendar.

Consumption was measured by asking women to bring their bottle to follow-up ANC visits, weighing it on a calibrated scale, and calculating tablets consumed since the previous visit from a per-tablet weight. This is believed to be a more reliable measure than self-reporting from the women receiving MMS.
Key indicators were distribution counts, MMS consumption, and anemia screening and treatment, all recorded by providers in the MMS-specific register.
The pilot's central question was whether this delivery model results in pregnant women consuming MMS at levels likely to achieve meaningful health benefits.

blocks.text: Compliance was calculated as tablets consumed divided by days elapsed since the previous visit. In approximately 38% of recorded patient-visits the calculated value exceeded one tablet per day. As consumption above one tablet daily is not plausible, these values were capped at one per day, to avoid inflating the result. No adjustment was applied to the remainder of the dataset.
Number of ANC visits recorded in the MMS register per enrolled woman:

Return rates in the MMS register run below what routine reporting would suggest. DHIS2 data for the same facilities over the same months shows non-return closer to 10%, against the 63.4% single-visit share recorded here. We attribute the difference to the completeness of a newly introduced register relative to established routine reporting, given the patient volumes health workers manage and the additional paperwork involved. Actual attendance is therefore likely higher than the register reflects.
Because women with only one recorded visit have no consumption measurement, we projected consumption assuming it follows the lowest consumption patterns observed among women with two or more visits.

blocks.label: The team's conclusion
blocks.text: The pilot has demonstrated that the delivery model achieves near-universal distribution with a reliable supply chain, and that observed consumption supports a cost-effectiveness case that clears Evidence Action's bar. We recommend proceeding to expansion. We expect consumption to improve further as health workers gain experience with the counseling protocol.
The cost-effectiveness model
Prepared by the cost-effectiveness team. Current program scenario: full rollout across Federal Capital Territory and Oyo.
At $292/DALY, the program clears Evidence Action's cost-effectiveness bar ($690/DALY, though most Evidence Action programs are far below this cost per DALY).

blocks.text: Treatment effects. The model applies Evidence Action point estimates, selected across the available meta-analyses.

Anemia-addressing benefit accrual by iron consumption. The model was developed internally, modelled based on related peer-reviewed research, to estimate how anemia benefits accrue with cumulative iron consumed rather than with completion of a full course. Anemia is an important factor affecting birth outcomes, though not the sole factor. MMS is made up of 15 vitamins and minerals, including 30mg of iron per tablet. Share of full birth-outcome anemia-specific benefit attained:
Additional materials

A. Commodity supply and financing note (procurement team). UNIMMAP-formulation MMS is produced by a small number of qualified manufacturers. Unit costs fall meaningfully with volume, but lead times run long and orders are placed well ahead of need. Our pilot supply was donated. For any expansion we would be purchasing at commercial terms. The Federal Ministry of Health has integrated MMS into national guidelines but has not committed to financing commodity beyond the pilot period. Discussions on domestic financing are at an early stage.

B. Recently published external evidence (forwarded by the global MLE team). A study published this quarter reports on MMS delivered through community health workers in a South Asian setting, with monthly household resupply and direct observation of consumption at each contact. The study reports 91% adherence and birth outcome improvements consistent with the meta-analytic estimates.

C. Health worker feedback on the MMS register (from pilot supervision). Of health workers surveyed at pilot facilities, 85% reported the new MMS register was manageable alongside their existing workflow, and 78% said they would prefer to continue using it over the previous IFA recording process. Several noted that on busy days they complete register entries in batches at the end of the day rather than at the time of each visit, and reported confidence in their recall.
The decision before you

No option involves withdrawing from where we operated the pilot. The choice is what we do beyond that. You must provide your recommendation based on what the evidence supports; expertise in local politics and donor willingness is not required. You must select only one, name an interval before you would expect another gating decision, and define your learning agenda for that period.
Option 1: Hold at the pilot footprint with a learning agenda, do not scale. Use the period to strengthen what we know about the delivery model before committing further.

items: 90 facilities, 52,000 women per year
$292 per DALY averted, $7.43 per woman initiated
Existing funding covers this footprint

blocks.text: Government momentum, pregnant women attending other ANCs, and donor interest on hold while we wait to learn more.
Option 2: Expand footprint within Nigeria. Full scale-up in existing states of operation plus a new third state: FCT, Oyo, Jigawa. Totals for the full three-state footprint:

items: 1,449 facilities, 1,985,558 women over three years
$255 per DALY averted, $5.21 per woman initiated
Requires new fundraising, not currently committed

blocks.text: Cost-effectiveness improves because many programmatic costs are largely fixed and spread across a larger population. The model applies a 20% benefit reduction to Jigawa to reflect poorer care-seeking behavior relative to the pilot states. The Federal Ministry has expressed strong interest in a multi-state footprint, and MMS is already in national guidelines.
Option 3: Maintain funded Nigeria footprint and expand into New Country. Maintain existing footprint within FCT and Oyo, and open a first program in New Country.

items: Approximately 1.1 million women in New Country over three years
Estimated $185 per DALY averted in New Country, $6.90 per woman initiated
A donor has offered to fully fund three years in New Country. The commitment is restricted to that geography.

blocks.text: New Country carries a substantially higher burden, driving better cost-effectiveness: low birth weight prevalence of 13% against Nigeria's 7%, anemia prevalence in pregnancy of 68% against 56%, and higher neonatal mortality. The New Country estimate applies the consumption distribution observed in the Nigeria pilot and the same 75% initiation assumption. Delivery costs are estimated by using Nigeria actual costs as a proxy. ANC attendance in New Country is later and less frequent than in Nigeria. MMS is not yet in New Country's national treatment guidelines.
What we are asking

Question 1: Gating criteria (1 page). Evidence Action has stage gates for approving new programs and for moving from pilot to scale, but no consistent standard for the decision that comes next: whether to hold a launched program or expand it, and on what evidence. The CEO has asked that your recommendation come with the beginnings of one. Set out the criteria that should govern this decision, designed so they could be applied to the next program and not only to this one. Include the evidence conditions a program should be required to satisfy at a gate at this stage.
Question 2: Your read of the evidence (1 to 2 pages). What is your assessment of the evidence presented to you from the pilot?

items: For each criterion you proposed above, state whether the MMS pilot passes, fails, or is indeterminate against it.
Be specific about what in this evidence you would rely on, what you would qualify, and what you would discount completely.

The projection that women consume an average of 117 tablets rests on an assumption about the women with no consumption data. Recompute that projection under a different assumption of your choosing. State the assumption, show your arithmetic.
What is your probability that true average consumption through term is below 100 tablets? What would move that number most?

blocks.text: Question 3: Recommendation (under 1 page). Which option do you think the evidence supports, and why, assessed against the criteria you have just set out? If you make any assumptions please name them clearly. Also include:

items: The one thing that, if it resolved differently, would change your recommendation.
One thing you know is unresolved and are choosing to live with, and why that is acceptable.

blocks.text: Question 4: Next gate and learning agenda (1 to 2 pages; a table is fine). Name the interval before you would expect the next gating decision on this program. If your recommendation is followed, what will we know at that gate that we do not know now, and how will we come to know it?

items: Be specific about method, and assume the agenda has to be executable within the interval you named.
Cover both what we need to learn to make the next gate decision and what we need to learn to run the program better in the meantime.
For each item, say what it costs us in money or in health worker time.

path_a.heading: MMS Nigeria: Response to the Program

blocks.text: Overview

Welcome to Stage 2, the final stage. Your Stage 1 response has been submitted and cannot be revised. Estimated time: 60 to 90 minutes. Use any format you prefer: write your response below or attach it as a PDF or Word document. Continue to disclose any AI tools used at the end of your response.
Scenario
You circulated your recommendation on Monday. The Program Director for MMS Nigeria has replied to you, copying the Nigeria Country Director and the EVP, Programs.

blocks.label: Memo. To: EVP, Evidence. From: Program Director, MMS Nigeria. Cc: Nigeria Country Director; EVP, Programs. Re: MMS expansion recommendation
blocks.text:
Thank you for the thorough review. I want to be direct about where I disagree, because I think the stakes of holding are being underweighted.

The pilot set out to establish whether we could get MMS into pregnant women's hands at scale through government ANC. We moved distribution from around 5 percent to 99.4 percent with no stockouts across 90 facilities. That is the thing we were testing, and it worked.

On consumption, I accept the register data is imperfect. Imperfect data is what we always have. But the underlying question of whether MMS outperforms IFA is not open. Four separate meta-analyses agree on the direction. We are not being asked to believe something speculative.

What concerns me is the standard being applied. We have programs at scale today that were expanded on considerably less than what this pilot produced. If the new bar is longitudinal consumption data of a quality we have never previously achieved anywhere, we should say so openly and apply it to everything, but then we must accept that it will stop much of what we do.

The costs of holding are concrete and they are being treated as if they were zero. The Federal Ministry put MMS into national guidelines and is asking us about a multi-state footprint now. That window does not stay open indefinitely, and if we signal hesitancy they will move on with other partners. We have developed training for health workers across the pilot LGAs and could easily apply those developed materials to new health workers. And every month we hold, women attending ANCs in expansion areas receive IFA rather than MMS. We have evidence that shows that to be a worse outcome.

I am not asking you to declare the consumption question resolved. I am asking that we not treat an unresolved measurement question as a reason to stop the progression of a program that is working.

Happy to discuss live. I want to land on something we can both support.
What we are asking
Please respond to the three items below. Aim for approximately two to three pages total.

items: Question 1: Your response. Write your reply to the Program Director. Be clear about where you concede and why, and where you hold and why.
Question 2: To the CEO. Write a note to the CEO on where this stands, where you see points of ongoing disagreement, and what, if anything, you need from her.

Question 3: Talking points. You will need to discuss this with your team internally, and possibly with external government and donor partners. This does not need to be polished, but draft a few bullets to guide your response. What do we know and what do we not know?

Scenario
You circulated your recommendation on Monday. The Program Director for MMS Nigeria has replied to you, copying the Nigeria Country Director and the EVP, Programs.

blocks.label: Memo. To: EVP, Evidence. From: Program Director, MMS Nigeria. Cc: Nigeria Country Director; EVP, Programs. Re: MMS expansion recommendation
blocks.text:
Thank you for this, and for backing the move to scale-up across our existing states and adding Jigawa. We are aligned on direction and I appreciate you getting there quickly.

Where I want to push is on the learning agenda attached to the recommendation, which I do not think we can absorb as written.

The binding constraint in our facilities is not money, it is health worker time. A first ANC visit already runs one to two hours and covers a broad set of clinical and counseling topics. Our health workers took on the MMS register willingly, but they told supervision teams it adds steps to a workflow that was already full. What you are proposing goes materially beyond that, and in most facilities it will require dedicated staff time we do not currently fund.

Where it does cost money, that money is not free. Every dollar spent measuring is a dollar not spent reaching women, and we are asking donors to fund an expansion we have not yet raised against. I would want to see the case that each measurement activity changes a decision we would otherwise get wrong, rather than that it improves what we know in general.

There is also a relationship dimension I do not think we should skip past. We are going to the Federal Ministry to propose expanding a program while simultaneously building an apparatus premised on not trusting our own reporting on it. I can make that case if I have to, but it is a harder conversation than it sounds, and we need the Ministry's goodwill for considerably more than MMS over the next two years.

My proposal is that we proceed with the scale-up using the current operating and assessment model, and revisit the learning agenda approach in year two once the expansion has bedded in. If there are one or two things you consider genuinely non-negotiable, tell me which and I will find a way to resource them.

Happy to discuss live. I want to land on something we can both support.

path_c.heading: MMS New Country: What the Evaluation Found

blocks.text: Overview

Welcome to Stage 2, the final stage. Your Stage 1 response has been submitted and cannot be revised. Estimated time: 60 to 90 minutes. Use any format you prefer: write your response below or attach it as a PDF or Word document. Continue to disclose any AI tools used at the end of your response.
Scenario

Time has passed. It is now the point at which you said, in Stage 1, that this decision should next be revisited. Evidence Action maintained the funded footprint in Nigeria and proceeded into New Country as you advised, funded by the donor, and the program has been operating at the planned footprint throughout.

An externally-led evaluation in New Country, which Evidence Action supported but did not run, has now reported. It collected consumption data independently of our registers, through household visits to a random sample of enrolled women.
What the evaluation found

items: Consumption in New Country came in materially below the distribution the model assumed, which was carried over from the Nigeria pilot. A substantial share of enrolled women consumed little or nothing after their first ANC visit.
Low birth weight prevalence in the program areas proved lower than the DHS vintage used in our modeling indicated, reducing the absolute burden available to avert.
Delivery cost per woman at operating scale has run above the figure estimated by analogy to Nigeria.

blocks.text: Taken together, the program in New Country is well below Evidence Action's cost-effectiveness bar. We have spent substantially, and the donor commitment has been largely drawn down.

blocks.label: The Program Director's position
blocks.text: I do not think this evaluation is the end of the story. The sampled population is not comparable to where we are strongest, we are mid-course on a delivery model that is still bedding in, and the government relationship we have built here is real and took two years. Stopping now spends that relationship for nothing and tells the Ministry we are not a serious partner. My view is that we adjust the model and continue.
The CEO has asked for your read before the Global Leadership Team discusses it next week.
What we are asking
Please respond to the three items below. Aim for approximately two to three pages total.

items: Question 1: Your response. Write your response to the Program Director's position on continuing. Be clear about what you accept and what you do not.

Question 2: To the CEO. Write the email to the CEO. Address whether the decision was right at the time, given what was known, and what you recommend now. If you believe some part of our process or performance failed, name it and explain why.

Question 3: Talking points. You will need to discuss this with your team internally, and possibly with external government and donor partners. This does not need to be polished, but draft a few bullets to guide your response. What do we know and what do we not know?
